newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian government defends race record.
newsitem.headline: Australian government defends race record.

text.p: An Australian minister smarting at British media criticism of Australia's race record defended his country on Thursday as the most tolerant on earth.
Prime Minister John Howard arrived in London on Wednesday for an official visit to be greeted by strong criticism in leading London newspapers over his handling of race issues.
"Australia is the most racially tolerant nation on earth," Howard's Aboriginal Affairs Minister John Herron retorted in a radio interview.
"I'd invite any Englishman or Englishwoman to come out here at have a look at the place and see for themselves rather than look at some advertisement in the newspaper."

Australian church, union, human rights and community groups have published full-page advertisements in London papers urging Prime Minister Tony Blair and Queen Elizabeth to press Howard over race and Australia's treatment of indigenous Aborigines.

British broadsheets the Independent, the Guardian and the Daily Telegraph ran articles on Wednesday criticising the conservative Australian leader's Aboriginal affairs policies and his handling of race row politician Pauline Hanson.

Howard is under fire at home for refusing to apologise for an official policy that continued up to 1970 to take Aboriginal children from their families and for his planned solution to a land rights row between Aborigines and graziers.

"Mr Howard is struggling against widespread criticism of his handling of Aboriginal affairs, dissatisfaction from the business community over a stalled economy, and concern that he has failed to control the spreading racial debate driven by the maverick independent politician Pauline Hanson," the Daily Telegraph said.
The Guardian said Howard's indecision and weakness had allowed Hanson -- a far-right populist opposed to immigration, Aboriginal welfare and foreign investment -- to flourish.
Hanson has struck a chord with voters disillusioned by the major parties and worried by stubbornly high unemployment, a manufacturing recession and sluggish economic growth.

Opinion polls show her newly-formed One Nation Party has up to 10 percent support, enough to make it the third power in Australian politics if that is maintained to the next election, due by mid-1999.
Howard told government backbenchers this week he would use a high-profile speech in London on Monday to denounce Hanson as an extremist with little popular support.

Political opponents, including Hanson, have criticised the devoted cricket fan for his 16-day trip to London, Washington and New York, which includes three cricket engagements and a baseball match, but just 45 minutes with Blair.
